why_not_adjudicable: These are v1 reviews. The current schema (v2) requires per-sample contextual-validity verdicts, exact clause coverage and dispatch-bound provenance, which a v1 reviewer was never asked for and which therefore cannot be recovered from a v1 record without inventing them. Every node listed here still owes a fresh blind re-review. This file exists so that the previous programme's findings remain visible as a QUEUE while none of them counts as evidence.
required_work: 151 node(s) need a fresh blind review filed at schema_version 2. Rebuild a packet with: python -m backend.app.practice_gen.validation.judgment_packets --node <node_id>

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The interview act itself is the object of the items: whom to ask, what to ask, what to do right after an answer, and what topic is being collected. Seed 44's key, Ask each classmate one by one and record their answers, is exactly the procedure the competency names, and the one-variable restriction holds throughout (one question per interview).

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Collection is sampled across its whole arc for a six-year-old: choosing respondents, posing the single question, recording a response, tallying with marks, and totalling one category. Both the procedural side and the recording side of a simple interview appear rather than only the easy identify-the-topic form.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Stems stay at one or two short clauses, respondent counts stay at four or five, and no item asks for anything beyond recognising and counting repeated answers. Grade 1 Quarter 3 pupils meeting data for the first time can handle this load.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: All ten samples are single-select multiple choice. A competency whose verb is collect ought to include at least one item where the pupil produces the record - fills a tally sheet or writes the counts - rather than only picking a pre-written record from four choices; the tally item at seed 600 comes closest but still only asks which of four printed mark-strings is right.

competency_alignment.rationale: Harder seeds genuinely ask more of the interview skill (counting repeated responses across four named respondents, choosing the correct two-category record) while easier ones name the topic. The axis that grows is data-handling load, not some unrelated dressing.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Sample sizes of four and five respondents, with category counts never above four, sit well inside what a Grade 1 pupil can survey and record in one sitting, and no numeric demand exceeds simple counting.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Each item does ask the pupil to build the graph, and the one-picture-per-item instruction is the correct rendering of a pictograph without a scale - no symbol ever stands for more than one unit, which is the whole point of the without a scale clause.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The source data is always handed over already counted, as a ready list of four labelled numbers. Nothing asks the pupil to build a picture graph from tally marks, from a table, or from a set of objects, so the only route into a pictograph that Grade 1 ever practises here is transcription of printed numerals.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Four categories with counts from 1 to 5 is a sensible drawing load for this age, the label sets (days, fruits, subjects, sports) are all familiar, and the instruction sentence is short and imperative.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Across ten seeds there is exactly one item shape. The three opening phrasings - the survey shows, look at the data, complete the picture graph - are cosmetic rewordings of the same sentence, and what actually changes from seed to seed is the label list, the picture symbol and four small numbers. Nothing varies the number of categories, the orientation of the graph, or the direction of the task.

competency_alignment.rationale: The key is a verbatim copy of the counts already printed in the stem, so no seed is harder than any other in any way that involves presenting data; the difficulty axis that does move is which emoji is drawn, which is unrelated to the competency.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Counts are capped at 5 per row, appropriate when every picture equals one unit - a taller bar of symbols would make an unscaled pictograph unwieldy for a Grade 1 hand.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Reading single rows and computing differences is squarely interpretive, but two stems ask for the total number of sports shown and the total number of colors shown while the keys (13 and 10) are sums of the tallies, not counts of the categories named. A pupil who answers the question as literally worded - how many sports - is marked wrong.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Three interpretive moves appear (read one row, compare two rows, total all rows) but the most basic pictograph question of all is missing: no sample asks which category has the most or the fewest, and none asks a yes/no comparison. That omission leaves the easiest and most common interpretation demand unsampled.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Counting symbols, taking a difference of at most 4, and summing four small rows to a total under 16 are within reach at Quarter 3 of Grade 1, and each stem is a single short question after Look at the picture graph.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Although every item is a four-option read question - correct, since the graph must be on screen - the underlying task genuinely rotates among row-reading, difference-finding and totalling, and the subject matter moves across fruit, books by day, animals, flowers, grade levels, sports and colours.

competency_alignment.rationale: The progression from reading one row, to comparing two, to summing the whole graph is a real ladder of interpretation difficulty built on this competency rather than on arithmetic dressing.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Row values stay small enough to count symbol by symbol and the largest total shown is 15, which keeps the summing items inside Grade 1 addition even though the competency itself states no ceiling.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The direction of transfer is right: the pictograph is the given, the table is the product, and instructions such as Count the pictures in each row of the pictograph make the counting step explicit rather than handing the pupil the numbers.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Every sample presents a full four-row graph and asks for all four table cells. There is no partially completed table to finish, no graph with a different number of rows, and no item where one row must be checked against a total - so organising is only ever practised at one fixed size and in one fixed completeness.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Counting up to five identical pictures in a row and writing the numeral in a table cell is a fair Quarter 3 demand, and the category labels used - days, subjects, sports, flowers - need no reading beyond a Grade 1 sight vocabulary.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Three stem wordings rotate, ending variously with Fill in the table with the correct counts or a listing of the four row labels, but structurally the ten items are one task. No seed reverses the direction (table back to graph) or changes the response mode away from typing four counts.

competency_alignment.rationale: What differs between an early seed and a late one is the label family and the four underlying numbers; the organising demand itself is identical at every seed, so there is no progression that deepens this competency.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Per-row counts never exceed 5 and the table is always four rows deep, which matches an unscaled pictograph a Grade 1 pupil can read picture by picture without losing place.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Most stems hand the pupil the defining property in words before asking the question - a party hat is described as shaped with 3 straight edges, a chalkboard as having 4 straight edges and opposite edges are equal. The pupil can answer by matching a counted word to a shape name without ever looking at the figure, which is not the identification the competency asks for.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Triangle, rectangle and square all appear as keys, but the different orientation clause is carried by a single sample, the triangular sign that is turned upside down. No rotated square, no tilted rectangle, and different size is signalled only by the adjectives small and large rather than by any contrast between two sizes of the same shape.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Vocabulary stays at edges, corners and the three shape names, the contexts (party hat, chalkboard, floor tile) are everyday Filipino classroom objects, and one-sentence stems suit the opening quarter of Grade 1.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: The party hat stem recurs verbatim at three of the ten seeds and the chalkboard stem at two more, so half the sample set is two sentences. Real variety here would mean the same shape shown at different tilts and sizes, which is precisely what the competency names and what the repetition crowds out.

competency_alignment.rationale: Between seeds the thing that reliably changes is the order of the four options, not the size or orientation of the shape being identified, so the seeds do not form a progression that builds toward recognising a shape however it is turned.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: No numeric range is in play for a shape-naming competency; the only numbers used are the edge counts 3 and 4, which are exactly the attributes of the three named shapes.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The comparisons themselves are on target, but the option lists undercut them. Asked which shape has the same number of sides as a square, the pupil is offered they are different and neither alongside two shape names - two of the four choices cannot answer a which-shape question at all, which narrows a four-way item to a two-way guess.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both features the competency names are exercised: sides appear in the more-sides and same-number-of-sides items, corners in the fewer-corners item and in the tilted square and flat rectangle question. More, fewer and same are all represented as relations.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Comparing two named shapes on a single attribute, with answer text as short as Yes, both have 4 corners, is a reasonable first-quarter Grade 1 demand and needs no counting beyond four.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Eight of the nine samples are three recycled sentences about triangle-versus-rectangle sides or square-versus-triangle corners. Only the tilted square and flat rectangle item introduces orientation, and no item compares three shapes or asks the pupil to justify by counting a drawn figure.

competency_alignment.rationale: The seeds that differ do so by switching the attribute under comparison (sides versus corners) and the direction of the relation, both of which are axes internal to distinguishing shapes by feature.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Side and corner counts of 3 and 4 are the only quantities involved, which is precisely the range the three named 2-dimensional shapes generate.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Composing and decomposing are both genuinely asked, but one composition item is under-determined: two triangles placed together, matching their longest straight edges is given a key of rectangle while square sits in the same option list, and nothing in that stem rules the square out. Seed 502 shows the generator can disambiguate by describing the result as a 4-sided shape with equal sides, which makes the looser stem a defect rather than an unavoidable ambiguity.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both verbs of the competency are worked in both directions and all three shapes take part: triangles joined into a rectangle and into a square, squares joined into a rectangle, a rectangle cut into two squares, a square cut on a slant into two triangles, and a rectangle halved into two rectangles.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The language of cutting across its width and placing side by side is concrete and matches what a Grade 1 pupil does with paper shapes; no item requires imagining more than two pieces at once.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: The set alternates between items with a figure to inspect and items answered from the description alone, and it mixes joining actions with cutting actions and slant cuts with straight cuts, so presentation genuinely rotates rather than repeating one frame.

competency_alignment.rationale: Difficulty moves along a line that belongs to this competency - from naming the result of an obvious side-by-side join, to reading a diagonal cut, to recognising that two triangles can make either a rectangle or a square depending on the pieces.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Every composition and decomposition involves exactly two pieces, which is the level at which Grade 1 composing and decomposing of plane shapes is expected to operate.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Both objects of the competency are measured: the length of a single object (paintbrush, pencil) and the separation between two objects, each expressed as a count of a non-standard unit rather than centimetres.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Three different non-standard units are used - paperclips, hands and crayons - and the two required situations, measuring one object and measuring a gap between two, are both present with several object pairs.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Reading off a count of repeated units from a picture, with the cloze frame the distance between them is ___ paperclips, asks for nothing beyond counting, which is right for Quarter 2 of Grade 1.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Six of the nine samples are the one sentence about two objects placed apart with a blank for the unit count; only the two how-long questions break that pattern, and nothing asks the pupil to choose an appropriate unit or to measure the same object in two different units.

competency_alignment.rationale: Across seeds the measured value shifts between roughly 1 and 11 but nothing else about the measuring demand changes, so there is no progression - no longer object needing more units laid end to end, no item where the units must be counted past a partial unit.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Every one of the nine option sets contains 20 while every key lies between 1 and 11, and 20 is never the answer. A fixed out-of-range decoy in every item both misrepresents what a plausible non-standard measurement looks like and lets a pupil eliminate a quarter of the choices without measuring anything - and in the shortest items, such as the one whose options are 1, 2, 20, 3, it effectively reduces the question to a three-way choice among adjacent small numbers.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The comparisons are correct and both lengths and distances are compared, but half of each option list is unreachable: asked which is longer, 6 paperclips or 4 paperclips, the pupil is offered 5 and 7, values that appear nowhere in the stem. Every sample carries two such impossible options, so each item is really a two-way decision dressed as a four-way one.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both directions of comparison are sampled in roughly equal measure - shorter and longer each appear several times - and the comparison is applied both to object lengths in paperclips and to walked distances in blocks and hands.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Two-sentence distance setups naming a bench, a tree and a gate, followed by a single which-is-shorter question, are well within Grade 1 Quarter 2 reading and reasoning; no computation is required, only ordering two counts.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: The set carries a bare two-quantity comparison alongside a short narrative comparison of two routes, and answers are collected both as a cloze blank and as a choice, so the presentation is not a single template.

competency_alignment.rationale: Seeds vary the closeness of the two quantities, from a wide gap like 2 against 6 down to adjacent counts like 6 against 7, which is a real difficulty axis for comparing measures rather than an unrelated one.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: All compared values sit between 2 and 9 units, a count a Grade 1 pupil can actually lay out with paperclips or pace out in blocks, and the competency sets no higher ceiling to exceed.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Every sample is a genuine problem in which a non-standard measurement must be operated on rather than merely read: how many hands longer one object is than another, how many steps were walked in all, and how many steps farther one place is than another.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both problem structures that lengths and distances support are generated - comparison by difference, and combination by sum, including the end-to-end item asking for their total length in paperclips - and the units rotate through hands, steps and paperclips.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Two given quantities, one operation, values no larger than 10 and a sum capped at 10 keep the reasoning to a single step, which is the right ceiling for Quarter 2; the settings, such as walking from the gate to the tree to the bench, are familiar.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Four distinct problem frames appear - two objects compared, a two-leg walk totalled, two distances from the teacher's desk compared, and two objects laid end to end - and answers are taken both as a typed blank and as a selection.

competency_alignment.rationale: The harder seeds widen the gap between the two measures or push the total toward 10, and the operation required shifts between difference and sum; both are axes of this problem-solving competency rather than decoration.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Measures run from 2 to 8 units with results between 1 and 10, comfortably inside Grade 1 addition and subtraction and inside what can genuinely be measured with hands, steps or paperclips.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Each item supplies an initial facing direction, applies a named turn, and asks for the resulting direction, which is exactly the structure the competency describes; every key I checked is correct, including a right-facing arrow given a quarter turn counter-clockwise ending up facing up.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Half turns and quarter turns clockwise are each sampled several times, but counter-clockwise appears in exactly one of the nine items. A competency that names two rotation directions explicitly should not leave one of them represented by a single seed, since a pupil practising here will almost never meet the harder direction.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The stems are two short sentences, the four answers are the plain words up, down, left and right, and the supporting item defining a turn as the direction clock hands move gives the vocabulary an anchor suitable for Quarter 4 of Grade 1.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Apart from the one definition question, every sample is the same arrow sentence with a different starting direction. The competency speaks of objects being moved, which invites a chair, a pupil or a toy turning in place, and none of that context appears - nor does any item that runs the reasoning backwards by giving the result and asking for the turn.

competency_alignment.rationale: What changes between seeds is the starting orientation and the size of turn, both of which are the substance of this competency, and all four cardinal starts are used rather than only the easy upward one.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Turns are restricted to the half and quarter the competency names, with no eighth turns or multi-turn chains, so the generated range matches the stated bound exactly.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Both verbs are served by distinct item types: reading is asked as What time does the clock show, and writing is asked by having the pupil set the clock to a stated time, with the analog face implied in both directions.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: All three granularities named are present - exact hours such as 5:00 and 9:00, half hours such as 7:30 and 12:30, and quarter hours in both forms, quarter past in the 2:15 and 6:15 reading items and quarter to in 5:45 and 3:45.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Two of the three reading items put an off-curriculum time among the choices - 2:10 in one option list and 9:25 in another. A Grade 1 pupil taught only hour, half hour and quarter hour has no basis for reading a minute hand at ten or twenty-five past, so those decoys test a skill the competency deliberately withholds at this level.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: The set alternates between recognising a displayed time from four choices and constructing a time on the clock face, and the times sampled span morning and midday hours including the 12 o'clock case.

competency_alignment.rationale: Difficulty rises along the intended line, from whole hours to half past to the quarter positions, rather than by varying the hour number alone, and the reading items pit the answer against neighbouring hours which is the real confusion to train out.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Hours stay within the 12-hour analog face, minute values are confined to 00, 15, 30 and 45 in the keys, and no 24-hour or minute-level precision creeps in.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The items ask for sequence position directly - which day comes right after Friday, which month comes right before December - which is the order relation the competency is about, and the keys are correct in every sample.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both cycles are sampled and both directions of traversal appear in each: days forward from Friday, Saturday, Tuesday and Wednesday and backward from Thursday and Wednesday; months forward from October and June and backward from December, September, July and June.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: A single short question naming one day or month, answered with another name, is an appropriate memory task for Quarter 4 of Grade 1, and no item requires counting several steps through the cycle.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: The answer is collected both as a typed blank and as a selection, and the sampled anchors move around the week and around the year rather than clustering at one point in either cycle.

competency_alignment.rationale: The month items are answerable without knowing month order at all. In five of the six, the three wrong choices are drawn only from January, February and March - for instance the item keyed November offers January, February and March beside it, and the item keyed August does the same. Whenever the key is not itself an early-year month, spotting the odd one out yields the answer, so the difficulty axis that actually distinguishes these seeds is decoy selection rather than the ordering skill being built. The day items, whose decoys include genuine near neighbours such as Thursday beside a key of Wednesday, show the generator is capable of better and makes the month behaviour a defect rather than a limitation.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Only the seven real weekday names and the twelve real month names are used, with no invented or out-of-cycle members, so the domain matches the competency exactly.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Both nouns of the competency are addressed against an actual calendar page: the day of the week for a given date, and the identification of which month the displayed page belongs to. Nothing is answerable without consulting the calendar shown.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Dates sampled sit early, mid and late in the month - the 1st, the 2nd, the 6th, the 12th, the 19th, the 21st, the 23rd, the 25th and the 30th - so the pupil must track across several week rows rather than only reading the top line, and the month-identification case gets its own seeds.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Locating a numeral in a grid and reading up to its column heading is a visual-scan task with no arithmetic, well matched to Quarter 4 of Grade 1, and each stem is one sentence after the instruction to look at the calendar.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Two genuinely different questions are asked of the same artefact - find the weekday of a date, and name the month of an unlabelled page - and the calendar pages themselves rotate through most of the year rather than reusing one month.

competency_alignment.rationale: Later seeds move the target date deeper into the month, which is the real difficulty axis for calendar reading, and the month-naming items require reading the page layout rather than a caption; both build this competency directly.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: All dates fall within the true length of the month named and I verified the weekday keys against the 2025 calendar - February 1 as Saturday, May 23 as Friday, July 2 as Wednesday, November 19 as Wednesday, April 30 as Wednesday and January 12 as Sunday are each correct, so the underlying calendar data is sound.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The clock and calendar items are posed as situations to resolve rather than as readings - a break that starts at 9:00 and lasts a quarter of an hour (15 minutes), a snack time measured from start to finish, a gap counted between a school program and an exhibit - which is the problem-solving the competency calls for.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The competency lists five things problems may involve and one of them, days in a week, generates no problem at all. The only day-related samples ask what day of the week is May 21 and what day of the week is June 6 - calendar look-ups identical in shape to the calendar-reading competency's own items, requiring no elapsed-time or cyclic reasoning about a week. Hour, half hour, quarter hour and months in a year are all properly sampled, which makes the single missing sub-case a gap rather than a general weakness.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Each problem gives two facts and asks for one, minute quantities are glossed in parentheses where they appear, and the month gaps never exceed four, keeping every item to a single step that a Quarter 4 Grade 1 pupil can hold in mind.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Presentation rotates widely: a duration added to a start time, an end time given and the elapsed minutes asked, an elapsed span in whole hours, a month advanced by a count, and a month gap asked in the other direction - collected as selections, typed blanks and cloze answers.

competency_alignment.rationale: Two of the fifteen samples spend their seeds on plain calendar look-ups that ask no time question, so part of the generated range does not advance this competency at all; the remaining items do progress sensibly from quarter-hour to hour-scale to multi-month spans.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Times stay on a 12-hour clock with minute values confined to the quarter, half and hour marks, month intervals run from 2 to 4 within a single year, and the longest elapsed span asked is the three hours from 9:00 to 12:00.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Counting to 100 is exercised in three distinct senses - continuing a sequence such as 94, 95, 96, 97 with a blank, counting a large group of objects to a total, and locating a marked number - all of which are the competency's core act.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The competency spells out counting up or down and identifying a number that is 1 more or 1 less, and only the upward half is ever generated. All five sequence items ascend, the narrative item explicitly states counting forward by 1, and across nine samples no item counts backwards or asks for 1 less than a given number. Two of the four behaviours the competency names in parentheses are therefore unsampled, and a pupil could clear this node without ever counting down.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Four-term sequences with a single blank, and object counts presented as a large group with a stated total to verify, match the demands of Quarter 1 Grade 1; no item requires writing number words or operating on the numbers.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Four presentations are in play - a bare sequence, a number line with a mark to read, a pictured collection to count, and a named pupil narrating a count - and answers are taken both as a typed blank and as a choice.

competency_alignment.rationale: The axis that actually varies across seeds is the magnitude of the starting number, from the 30s to the 90s. Because direction is held fixed at forward, the seeds never get harder in the way this competency defines harder, and the decade-crossing case that makes counting up to 100 difficult is only incidentally touched.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Values reach into the 90s and the counted collections run to 64 and 78, so the stated ceiling of 100 is genuinely approached rather than the generator hovering in safe two-digit territory, and nothing exceeds it.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Both halves of read and write are generated as separate tasks - converting a numeral into words, as in the instruction to write 68 in words, and converting a spoken form such as ninety-eight back into digits - with true-or-false checks probing the same correspondence.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Every value sampled is a two-digit number from the mid-thirties upward. The teens, where the reading-and-writing confusion actually lives for six-year-olds, never appear, nor does any single-digit numeral, so the specific traps this competency exists to train are outside the generated set even though the direction coverage is even.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Hyphenated two-digit number words and short imperative stems are the right demand for Quarter 1, and the true-or-false framing, such as the claim that 35 is written in words as 'fifty-three', asks for a judgment rather than production, which lightens the load appropriately.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Three response modes appear across the eight samples and the direction of translation flips between them, so the pupil meets the correspondence from both ends rather than only decoding or only encoding.

competency_alignment.rationale: The decoys are built on the genuine misconceptions this competency targets - the digit reversal offering eighty-six against sixty-eight, and the neighbouring-decade confusion of seventy-three against eighty-three - so the difficulty sits on reading and writing rather than elsewhere.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: The ceiling of 100 is respected but never reached: the largest numeral written is in the nineties and 100 itself appears only inside a true-or-false claim as a wrong value, so the pupil is never asked to read or write the boundary number the competency names.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Representation is asked in both directions the competency implies - building a quantity with a model, as in the instruction to use base-10 blocks to show the number 35, and recognising a quantity from a model already shown on a number line or in blocks.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The stated variety of models is only partly realised: base-10 blocks and the number line carry all eight samples, with no bar model and no other concrete grouping, and the values used never drop below the mid-thirties, so the ten-and-ones structure of small two-digit numbers is never modelled.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Placing a dot on a number line and assembling tens and ones are the standard concrete-to-pictorial bridges for Quarter 1 of Grade 1, and each stem is a single imperative or a single question with no multi-step reasoning.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Two model families each appear in both a construct form and a read form - move the dot to show 99 on the number line against asking what number is marked on it - which gives the pupil four genuinely different encounters rather than one repeated frame.

competency_alignment.rationale: The block-reading item pits 83 against 38 and a plausible small value, which tests place value in the model itself, and the number-line items sit the target next to its immediate neighbours; both keep the difficulty on representation rather than on arithmetic.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Values run up to 99 with 100 present as an option on the number line item, so the stated ceiling is reached without being exceeded, and the quantities remain modellable in tens and ones.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Each sampled item does resolve a comparison of two numerals within 20, which matches the verb and the bound, but the competency wording names no symbols and all fourteen seeds demand symbolic notation; seeds 44 and 46 offer only the three signs as choices and no item anywhere asks the comparison in words such as greater than, so the notation load is carried into a competency that never asked for it.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: All three relations are genuinely produced: the greater case at seed 45 with 8 against 1, the less case at seed 603 with 1 against 2, and equality at seeds 502 and 601. Reversed orderings also appear among the distractor sets, so neither operand position is fixed.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Most stems are two short sentences with a concrete noun, which suits the first quarter of Grade 1. Seed 605 is not: it embeds a comparison question inside a stated answer inside a true or false judgement, three layers of indirection for a six year old who is still learning the signs themselves.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: The true or false variant is degenerate. Seeds 42, 500, 501, 600, 602 and 605 are keyed False with no exception, so six of the fourteen delivered items can be answered correctly by a pupil who never looks at the numerals. Word problem and pure numeral framings are otherwise both present.

competency_alignment.rationale: What tightens across the set is the discrimination itself: seed 45 separates 8 and 1 by a wide margin, seed 604 separates 18 and 17 by a single unit, and seeds 502 and 601 remove the gap entirely. That is the comparison skill being graded, not a side axis.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Operands span the whole stated interval, with 1 appearing at seeds 44, 45 and 602 and the ceiling of 20 reached at seed 501. On a span this small a flat spread is the right choice and that is what the seeds show.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Every sample asks for a full arrangement of a given set, and the response is the ordered list itself rather than a single pick, which is the precise act the competency describes; each key I checked orders its own set correctly.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The and vice versa clause is fully honoured - smallest to largest and largest to smallest each appear in roughly half the fourteen samples - and both three-element and four-element sets are generated, so set size is not held fixed at the easiest value.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Ordering three or four numbers below 21, with narrative items framed as a friend's collection of marbles, seashells or stickers, keeps reading short and the working memory demand appropriate for Quarter 1 of Grade 1.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Bare lists to arrange sit alongside counted collections attributed to named friends, and two distinct ordering response modes are used, so the pupil meets the same skill in both an abstract and a situational dress.

competency_alignment.rationale: Difficulty rises along axes that belong to ordering - from three items to four, and from well-spread sets like 9, 10, 8 to sets mixing a single-digit value with numbers in the high teens - rather than through unrelated context changes.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Every value falls between 1 and 20 with the ceiling itself used repeatedly as a set member, so the stated bound is exercised rather than avoided, and no value strays above it.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The competency is about describing the position of objects, but most samples are pure notation drills - asking which word describes the 5th position, or to write the symbol for the third position - with no object in sight. Only three of the twelve attach an ordinal to something positioned, such as pupils standing in a row or baskets placed in a row, so the object-anchored form the wording calls for is the minority case.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The stated span is well covered: 1st, 3rd, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th and 10th all appear as keys or targets, and both representations named in the competency, the symbol form and the word form, are produced rather than only recognised.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Recognition of denominations and their notations is well served, but the competency excludes centavo coins and the option lists reintroduce them through a cent symbol, offering forms like 20 with a cent mark and 100 with a cent mark. That is both outside the stated scope and not the notation Philippine centavos use.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Coins at one, five, ten and twenty and bills at twenty, fifty and one hundred all appear, and all three notation forms named or implied - peso symbol, words, and the code form asked by 'How is ₱100 written using the currency code PhP?' - are generated.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Each item asks for a single identification or a single translation between two ways of writing an amount, with no arithmetic, which is the right load for Grade 1 money work.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Direction of translation is varied properly: some items go from symbol to words, others from words to symbol, and others identify a piece from the number printed on it, covering both a coin and a bill.

competency_alignment.rationale: What changes between seeds is the denomination and which notation is being asked for, both of which are the substance of this competency rather than an incidental axis.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Stems stay at or below one hundred pesos as required, but distractors introduce ₱1000, ₱500 and ₱200 - real denominations above the stated ceiling, so a recognition task deliberately shows pupils money they are not meant to be learning yet.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Two of the sampled money number-line items are internally inconsistent. 'The dot is at ₱10 and it moves forward ₱1.' is keyed to the second option in a list reading 70 / 71 / 76 / 66, a set which does not contain eleven at all; another item starting at five pesos and moving forward ten pesos is keyed to eighty-five. The stem asks for one amount and the key answers a different one, with no correct choice available.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The competency covers bills and-slash-or coins, but the sampled totals are either all coins or all bills; no item totals a mixed handful of bills together with coins, which is the case the and-or phrasing exists to capture.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The composing tasks defeat themselves: 'Use coins and bills to make exactly ₱60. Use the fewest pieces possible.' is keyed to sixty, the number already printed in the stem, so nothing about choosing pieces or minimising their number is actually required or recorded.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Once the broken number-line items and the self-answering composing items are set aside, what remains is a small set of straightforward totalling questions, so the apparent breadth of presentation is not doing real work.

competency_alignment.rationale: Determining the value of a group of pieces is the target skill, but a large share of seeds instead exercise movement along a marked line, an axis that belongs to counting on rather than to valuing a collection of money.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Totals in the valid items reach one hundred pesos appropriately, but one option list offers 110 and 120 against a target of exactly one hundred, and the mismatched number-line items present amounts in the seventies and eighties that no part of their stem can produce.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Every item places one denomination against another and asks which is worth more or less, as in 'Which has a smaller value: 1 ₱5 coin or 1 ₱50 bill?', and each key names the correct piece.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both directions of the question are generated, coin-against-coin and coin-against-bill and bill-against-bill all occur, and the full denomination set from one peso to one hundred pesos is drawn on.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The comparison is single-step and the pieces are named in full, so the only demand is knowing the relative worth of two denominations, which is what Grade 1 money work is for.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Across fourteen samples there is exactly one sentence frame with only the two denominations and the greater-or-smaller word swapped; no item shows the money, embeds the comparison in a buying situation, or compares several pieces against one.

competency_alignment.rationale: The option lists weaken the ramp rather than strengthen it: 'They are equal' is offered constantly although two different denominations are never equal, and several options name pieces that appear nowhere in the stem, so wrong answers fall away without any comparison being made.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: No denomination above one hundred pesos is used in stems or options, so this node stays inside its ceiling - unlike the recognition node in the same quarter.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Each sampled item is a single-step money situation resolved by one addition or one subtraction, and the settings - a piggy bank, buying a snack at the sari-sari store, spending at the palengke - are recognisably Philippine and age-appropriate.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both branches of the competency's or-clause are present in quantity: money joined together from two sources or two purchases, and money spent or used from a starting amount.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Several sampled amounts demand regrouping that nothing in the preceding Grade 1 work provides - the pupil who 'used ₱39 to buy a notebook' from fifty pesos must break a ten, as must one spending eighty pesos less two, and a purchase of a fifteen-peso pencil with a fifteen-peso eraser carries the ones into a new ten. Every addition and subtraction competency shown earlier in this grade is explicitly restricted to work without regrouping.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Situations rotate through saving on two days, money in two pockets, receiving more from a family member, buying two items, and spending from a store of money, so the contexts are not one story retold.

competency_alignment.rationale: Difficulty increases through the size of the amounts and whether the two amounts sit close together, which sharpens money computation itself rather than substituting a different skill.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Stem amounts respect the hundred-peso ceiling, but option lists jump far past it with values like 820, 400 and 200 offered against problems whose answers are in the tens - amounts no pupil at this level should be weighing as plausible money.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The or-vice-versa requirement is genuinely met in both directions: some items build symbols from given counts, as in 'Create a picture graph where each 🍎 equals 10.', and others read a pictograph back into table counts, and the sampled keys divide or multiply by the stated scale correctly.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Tabular data and pictographs are both handled, but the competency's first listed input, raw data, never appears - no item starts from an unorganised tally or list that the pupil must first collate before graphing, so one named starting point is absent.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Scales of two, five and ten with four to six categories is a fair Grade 2 load, and every stem states the scale in words, as with 'The scale is 5: each symbol stands for 5 items.', rather than making pupils infer it.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: All eleven samples use the same constructed-response format; the stem wording rotates but the pupil always types a list of numbers, so there is no selection, judging or partially-built-graph variation anywhere in this node.

competency_alignment.rationale: The lever that moves between seeds is scale size and category count, both of which make scaled graphing genuinely harder, and the keys always require the scale conversion rather than a direct copy.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Data values top out around fifty and all are exact multiples of the stated scale, keeping the arithmetic inside Grade 2 multiplication and division by two, five and ten.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Most items do interpret displayed data, but the comparison questions are malformed: 'Which has the most colors: red, blue, green or yellow?' asks which colour has the most colours, when the intended question is which category has the greatest count. The same construction recurs with school subjects, so the stem does not ask what the key answers.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The competency names tabular form and pictographs, with and without scale, but of the eight samples only one reads a table and only one states a scale explicitly; the tabular strand and the scaled strand are each represented by a single item against six unscaled picture graphs.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The interpretive moves asked for - retrieve one value, find a difference, total a display - are each one or two steps with values in the tens, which is appropriate for Grade 2 Quarter 3.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: The question types vary usefully, but the response format does not: every sampled item is the same read-and-choose form, with no item asking a pupil to state a count, judge a claim about the graph, or compare two displays.

competency_alignment.rationale: Harder seeds ask for totals and differences rather than single retrievals and increase the number of categories, which deepens data interpretation rather than drifting into unrelated arithmetic practice.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Counts and totals stay in the tens and the scaled item uses a factor of five, so all the arithmetic sits inside what Grade 2 can carry out while reading a graph.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The describing half is done well, but the competency begins with representing, and no sampled item has a pupil draw, build, fold or assemble a circle, half circle or quarter circle. Every question is answered by selecting a name or a number, so half of the competency's verb pair is never exercised.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: All three figures are named and related to one another, including how many quarter-circles make a whole, but the descriptive attributes stay narrow - corners, straight sides and straight edges - while nothing addresses the curved side, size, or building a whole from parts in the other direction.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The reasoning is attribute recall and simple part-whole relation, and the comparison 'Which has more straight edges: a half-circle or a quarter-circle?' is correctly keyed, which is a fair discrimination for Grade 2.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Only two closely related choice formats appear, and 'What shape has no corners and no straight sides?' is regenerated verbatim across three separate seeds, so a pupil working through the node meets the same question repeatedly.

competency_alignment.rationale: The question set does move along a real conceptual line - naming a figure, deriving it by dividing a circle, counting parts that rebuild the whole, and holding identity under rotation - all of which belong to this competency.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: This competency sets no numeric ceiling, and the only numbers used are part counts of two and four together with a count of zero corners, all trivially inside Grade 2 number knowledge.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Composing and decomposing are both attempted, but roughly half the items list the parts inside the sentence and then ask how many simple shapes were used, so the pupil answers by counting nouns in the stem rather than by working with cut-outs or a grid.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: All six named shape families turn up somewhere in the set, and decomposition is genuinely represented as well as composition: a square cut corner to corner yields two triangles, and four quarter-circles are joined into a whole.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Sentences stay short, the counts involved never exceed four, and the shape vocabulary is the everyday Grade 2 set with no reference to angles, symmetry or measurement.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Presentation genuinely shifts across the set: grid-based figures, cut-out manipulations, name-the-resulting-shape items and count-the-parts items each appear more than once.

competency_alignment.rationale: The seed 600 item introduces a rotated composite shape yet still only asks for the number of simple shapes, so the added rotation changes nothing about the reasoning; difficulty is being varied on an orientation axis that the answer does not depend on.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: This competency states no numeric ceiling, and the incidental quantities used, part counts of one to four and grid sizes of four by two, sit comfortably inside Grade 2 range.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The samples do what the wording asks: they describe a multi-step movement in a single direction and require the resulting location, with the total displacement recovered from two consecutive steps.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Up and down slides appear only in items that ask for the name of the movement; every item that actually computes a landing position runs horizontally along marks or spaces, so the vertical case is never taken through to a described effect.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: One distractor list offers dilation alongside rotation and reflection. Dilation is nowhere near Grade 2 vocabulary and its presence teaches nothing, since no pupil at this level can reject it for a reason.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Four distinct demands are present across the seeds: where the figure ends up, what the movement is called, how far it travelled altogether, and whether size or shape is preserved.

competency_alignment.rationale: Harder seeds lengthen the two hops and shift the starting mark, which is exactly the quantity a pupil must track to describe a multi-step slide; nothing unrelated is being varied.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Slide lengths stay between one and four spaces and starting marks stay in single digits, which suits a Quarter 1 figure-on-a-grid task.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Comparison is well served, but the measuring half of this competency survives in only two items, both asking how long the object is. Eight of the ten samples hand the pupil two finished numbers, which is number comparison and needs no measuring tool at all.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Longer and shorter are both asked, and centimetres and metres both appear in the comparison items, yet the actual measuring items only ever request an answer in cm. Measuring a length in metres with a tool is never generated.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: One-step comparisons of two stated lengths, phrased in a single short sentence with familiar school objects, are well within what a Grade 2 Quarter 2 pupil can hold.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Three formatters are used but only two situations exist: two objects side by side, or two distances from a landmark. A measuring item where the pupil reads a scale appears just twice and with word-for-word identical wording both times.

competency_alignment.rationale: The step up in the later seeds is purely numeric, moving from a pencil at 10 and a ruler at 15 to distances of 82 and 37. Comparing larger integers is a number-sense axis, not a measurement one, so the added difficulty does not build this competency.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Object lengths sit in the tens of centimetres and distances in the tens of metres, which are believable magnitudes for the classroom objects and school landmarks named.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Identifying the right unit is handled thoroughly, but the competency also says to use that unit, and no sample ever asks the pupil to record or state a measurement once the unit is chosen. Every item stops at the choice.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both halves of the wording are populated: lengths of objects such as a spoon, a book and an eraser, and distances between two named places such as a gate and a library, with correct answers falling on both cm and m.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: A binary unit choice about familiar objects is appropriate here, and the magnitudes supplied in the blank-style stems, such as about 28 for a basketball court, give the pupil a usable cue without arithmetic.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: All twelve samples are the same two-way choice carrying the identical pair of filler options, either works and neither works. There is no ranking item, no odd-one-out, and no item where a wrong unit has to be corrected.

competency_alignment.rationale: The objects and distances chosen do move across the plausible range, from an eraser up to a basketball court and a house-to-church distance, so the progression tracks the size judgment this competency trains.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Each stated magnitude is realistic for the thing named, with small objects in the single and low double digits and distances of 50 and 150 for places that are genuinely that far apart.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Not one sample asks the pupil to estimate. Every item supplies an exact measurement and then asks for it rounded to the nearest 5 or nearest 10. Rounding a number already given is arithmetic on a numeral; estimating a length or distance is judging an unmeasured quantity, and that verb is never exercised.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Credit where due, all three combinations the wording names do occur: centimetres for objects, metres for objects, and metres for distance. But each is delivered through the one rounding task, so the sub-cases differ only in the unit word.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The values to be rounded stay between 14 and 35 and the rounding grain is 5 or 10, which is a reasonable arithmetic load for this grade even though it is the wrong task for this competency.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Twelve samples, one template. Each names an object or a school-to-school distance, states a measurement, and asks about how many units that is once rounded. Nothing varies except the noun, the number and the rounding grain.

competency_alignment.rationale: The only thing that changes between an easy and a hard seed is whether the target is the nearest 5 or the nearest 10. That is a rounding-precision axis; it does not deepen any estimating skill because no estimating is taking place.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Lengths in the twenties of centimetres and distances in the teens to thirties of metres are appropriate magnitudes for the rulers, storybooks, hallways and fences described.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Each sample is a genuine situation requiring a length or distance calculation, not a bare sum dressed up: objects laid end to end, two walked legs of a journey, and one place being farther from a gate than another.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both problem structures a competency like this needs are present in quantity. Joining appears through combined length and total distance walked, and comparing appears through how many metres farther and how many cm longer.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Single-step problems with two-digit quantities, named children and school landmarks match Quarter 2 of Grade 2; the subtraction cases such as 43 minus 19 involve regrouping but remain within reach.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Three distinct situation types recur across the seeds rather than one, and they alternate between centimetre object problems and metre distance problems, with both cloze and multiple-choice presentation.

competency_alignment.rationale: The later seeds raise the operands toward sums in the fifties and sixties while keeping the same length and distance reasoning intact, so difficulty grows along the competency rather than beside it.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Totals stay below one hundred, with objects sized in tens of centimetres and walks of a few tens of metres, all plausible for the classroom and schoolyard settings used.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The wording is about the duration of an event, yet no event is ever named. Each item gives two bare dates and asks how many days or weeks lie between them inclusive, so nothing is being described as having a duration.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Every weeks item spans an exact multiple of seven days, seven, fourteen or twenty-one, so a duration expressed as weeks together with leftover days never appears. The and part of the days and/or weeks wording is unproduced.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Counting inclusive days inside one month, with all spans kept within a single calendar page and never crossing a month boundary, is a fair demand for the fourth quarter of Grade 2.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: All fourteen samples share one formatter and one sentence, opening by directing the pupil to look at the month's calendar and closing with the same inclusive phrasing. Only the month, the two dates, and the choice of the word days or weeks ever change.

competency_alignment.rationale: Widening the date span and switching the requested unit from days to weeks are both legitimate ways to press on calendar reading, so the difficulty axis does belong to this competency even though the presentation does not vary.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: No span exceeds twenty-one days and every one lies inside a single month of 2025, which keeps the answers to small whole numbers of days or weeks as the competency implies.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Both verbs are served. Reading appears through items asking what time the clock shows, and writing appears through items asking the pupil to set the clock to a stated time, and a.m. or p.m. is attached in every single case.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The minute values cluster heavily on the hour, the half hour and forty-five past. Quarter past and five past never occur as targets, and only three distinct clock faces are ever read, so the reading direction is thinly covered against eight setting items.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: One item asks the pupil to set the clock to show 12:00 a.m. Midnight against noon is the single hardest a.m. and p.m. case there is, and dropping it in without scaffolding is a real stretch for this grade.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Only two presentations exist across twelve samples, and eight of them open with the same instruction to set the clock. No item connects a clock time to a daily routine or asks for a time to be written in words.

competency_alignment.rationale: The variation across seeds is the hour and minute values chosen and the a.m. or p.m. label, which is precisely what a pupil must control to read and write analog time.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Every target is a valid twelve-hour clock time on a five-minute boundary, and nothing strays into seconds or twenty-four-hour notation that would sit above this grade.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The samples land squarely on elapsed time and each of the three parenthesised sub-domains is exercised, including one where a class runs from 9:15 a.m. to 9:35 a.m. and one where a train journey's start must be recovered from its end and its length.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Minutes within an hour, whole hours within a day, days within a week, and timetables all appear, and the direction is varied too: some items ask for the duration, others for the end time, and one for the start time.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Durations stay under an hour for the minute items and the day-of-week items sit inside one week; the hardest case, a practice beginning at 10:25 a.m. and lasting 55 minutes, requires crossing an hour but nothing more.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Presentation genuinely shifts: a two-row bus timetable, a class schedule with subject names, plain start-and-end narratives, and weekday-spanning events all appear, across both cloze and multiple-choice.

competency_alignment.rationale: The harder seeds add a crossing of noon and an unknown start time rather than merely enlarging numbers, so the progression targets the elapsed-time reasoning itself.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Elapsed intervals run from twenty minutes up to six hours and event lengths from two to four days, all of which stay inside the minutes-in-an-hour, hours-in-a-day and days-in-a-week bounds the competency states.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Both the identifying and the explaining verbs are present. Some items ask which description best fits a rim or an edge, while others ask directly how a straight line differs from a curved one and why a given edge carries its name.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The three-dimensional half of the wording rests on a box and a ball only. No object is used that carries flat and curved surfaces at the same time, which is the case where a pupil must actually separate the two ideas rather than match one label.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Explanations are offered as complete short sentences about bending and not bending, which is the right level; the pupil recognises a correct explanation rather than composing one.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Every one of the nine samples is a multiple-choice item, and several close with the same request for the best description. There is no sorting task, no true-or-false, and no item that asks a pupil to find an example of their own.

competency_alignment.rationale: The variation across seeds moves between lines and surfaces and between naming and justifying, both of which are written into this competency rather than borrowed from a neighbouring one.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: This competency names no quantity or ceiling and the samples introduce none; the items remain entirely qualitative, which is correct for it.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The competency turns on measuring a figure with appropriate tools, and not one sample involves a tool or an unmeasured figure. Every item states the side lengths in the sentence and asks for the perimeter, which is arithmetic on given numbers rather than measurement.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The wording says plane figure in general, but only triangles, squares and rectangles are generated, and no item requires the pupil to obtain a dimension that was not already printed.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Adding three sides or doubling a length and a width, with side values no larger than twenty-one, is arithmetic a Grade 2 pupil in the fourth quarter can carry out.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Thirteen of the fourteen samples are the bare what is its perimeter frame, and the sample set duplicates the neighbouring find-the-perimeter node almost seed for seed, which means this node contributes no presentation of its own.

competency_alignment.rationale: Difficulty grows only by enlarging side lengths, moving a square's side from three up to seventeen. No seed increases any measuring demand, because there is no measuring demand to increase.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Side lengths run from one to twenty-one and perimeters top out below seventy, which keeps the addition inside a sensible range for this grade.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Each sample asks for the perimeter of one of the three figures the competency names, and the computations are correct throughout, including the triangle cases where three unequal sides must be summed.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Triangles, squares and rectangles are all generated repeatedly, with squares given by a single side, rectangles given by two sides, and triangles given by three, so each figure's own perimeter rule gets exercised.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The heaviest item asks for four times seventeen by repeated addition of a side, which is within the fourth-quarter range; all other cases are sums of small two-digit values.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Apart from a single garden item asking how much fencing goes all the way around, every sample is the identical bare question about a figure's perimeter. No diagram-led, missing-side or comparison presentation occurs.

competency_alignment.rationale: Across all fourteen seeds the four options sit within three units of the key, so a pupil who forgets to double a rectangle's sides finds no option matching their error and simply guesses; the option set is tuned to near-misses rather than to the misconceptions this competency should surface.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Side lengths stay between one and twenty-one, and the largest perimeter reached is sixty-eight, comfortably inside Grade 2 addition range.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Each item embeds a perimeter calculation in a real reason to go around a shape, asking how much fencing or edging is needed, and all three named figures carry their own situation.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Only the forward direction is generated. No sample supplies a perimeter and asks for a missing side, and none requires two steps such as comparing the fencing for two plots, which a solve-problems competency should reach.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: One-step problems in a garden setting with side lengths in metres and totals below seventy match what a fourth-quarter Grade 2 pupil can handle without scaffolding.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: There are effectively two sentences in the whole set, a rectangular or square garden needing fencing and a triangular flower bed needing edging. Every context is a garden, and no non-garden situation or diagram-led version appears.

competency_alignment.rationale: The later seeds enlarge the plot dimensions, up to a square garden with a side of seventeen metres, while holding the perimeter reasoning constant, so the ramp belongs to this competency.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Plot dimensions run from one to twenty-one metres and every total stays under seventy, which suits both the arithmetic level and the realism of a school garden.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Counting by ones is what this competency names, and several samples do not do it. Two items step by hundreds and one steps by twos, which is a different skill wearing the same what comes next wrapper.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Only forward counting is ever produced. Nothing counts backward, nothing counts on from a stated number toward a stated stop, and no item asks for a number that precedes the given run rather than follows it.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Four-term runs with one blank, in three-digit numbers, are well matched to the opening quarter of Grade 2, and the narrated version naming a child counting forward adds context without adding reading burden.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Four presentations occur across the seeds: a marked number line, a sequence with a trailing blank, a sequence introduced as a missing number, and a short narrative about someone counting aloud.

competency_alignment.rationale: Four of the fourteen samples are skip-counting sequences, including one running 0, 100, 200, 300 and another running 400, 500, 600, 700. Skip counting is the subject of a separate competency in this same quarter, so a substantial share of this node's difficulty is being varied on a neighbouring node's axis.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: The competency's ceiling is a thousand, yet the counting-by-ones items peak in the five hundreds; only the skip-counting intruders reach the upper hundreds, so the by-ones skill is never taken near the stated top of range.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Both directions the wording implies are generated: numerals turned into words, as with 470 and 587, and words turned back into numerals, as with seven hundred ten and three hundred fifty.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Numbers with an internal zero, such as 605 and 710, are included, which is good, but the whole set lives between 203 and 821. Nothing in the nine hundreds is generated and the thousand itself, the stated endpoint, never appears in either direction.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Three-digit number words with hyphenated tens such as eighty-seven are the correct load for Quarter 1 here, and no stem requires more than one number to be handled at a time.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Three formatters are used, but all three true-or-false instances are keyed False. A pupil who simply answers False every time scores full marks on that presentation, which makes it a degenerate variant rather than a third way of testing the skill.

competency_alignment.rationale: The distractors are built from real confusions this competency must clear, such as offering seventy-four against 470 and 53 against three hundred fifty, so the harder options probe place-value reading rather than an unrelated axis.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Every value handled is a three-digit numeral, which sits inside the range this competency sets even though the very top of that range goes untested.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The affirmative items genuinely illustrate the properties, but each negative one works by quietly substituting a different addend, as when 168 + 511 is set against 511 + 137. The pupil answers by spotting that a number changed, not by reasoning about order or grouping, so the false cases do not teach the property they are attached to.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: All three properties the wording lists are produced: adding zero in several forms, reordering two addends, and regrouping three addends with parentheses, each appearing across multiple seeds.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Parenthesised grouping is demanded by the competency itself, and the pupil is only ever asked whether two arrangements match rather than to evaluate both sides, which keeps the load manageable at this grade.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Four presentations occur: a true-or-false statement, a same-or-not comparison, a fill-in-the-total, and an error-detection item where a named pupil's answer must be checked.

competency_alignment.rationale: The zero property gets the richer treatment, appearing as a cloze and as an error-detection item, while order and grouping only ever arrive as a same-or-not judgment. Applying those two properties, as opposed to judging them, is never required.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Every sum stays at or below a thousand, with the largest pairs such as 976 plus 3 and 783 plus 213 approaching but not breaching that ceiling.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Both directions are attempted, building a model for a stated numeral and naming the numeral a model shows, but one options list places 20 among three three-digit choices, so that item can be narrowed without looking at the blocks at all.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The wording promises a variety of concrete and pictorial models, and exactly two ever appear: base-10 blocks and a number line. No place-value chart, bundled objects, money or expanded notation is generated.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Three-digit values represented on blocks or a marked line, with one instruction per item, are the right demand for the opening quarter of Grade 2.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Five of the eight samples are number-line items, and two of them repeat word for word the question asking what number is marked on the number line. The blocks presentation carries the remaining three.

competency_alignment.rationale: The numerals chosen deliberately include hard representation cases such as 203 with an empty tens column and 470 with an empty ones column, which is the right axis for a representation competency.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: All eight values are three-digit numerals between 203 and 821, sitting inside the thousand ceiling this competency sets.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The samples do what skip counting requires, completing a four-term run at a constant step, and the runs are placed so that some cross a hundred boundary, as with the sequence ending 298 and continuing to 300.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The competency names six step sizes and only five are generated. Twos, fives, tens, twenties and fifties all appear, but not a single sample counts by 100s. Ironically the hundreds runs surface in the neighbouring count-to-1000 node instead, so this sub-case is not merely rare here, it is absent.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: A four-term run with one blank is the right structure for Quarter 1, and the narrated version about someone counting forward by five from 875 adds a context without lengthening the reasoning.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Three presentations recur: a marked number line, a sequence with a trailing blank, and a short story about a child counting aloud, spread across cloze, multiple-choice and read-based formats.

competency_alignment.rationale: Difficulty varies by step size and by where the run sits relative to a hundred boundary, both of which are the genuine sources of difficulty in skip counting.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: The competency bars going beyond a thousand and nothing does; the highest sequence ends at 895 and the fifties run stops at 750.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: Every sample is a genuine ordering task with a correctly sorted key, and the and vice versa clause is honoured by items that ask for largest to smallest as often as smallest to largest.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both directions appear repeatedly, set sizes range from three to five numbers, and the thousand itself is included in several sets, so the top of the stated range is actually exercised rather than approached.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Arranging at most five three-digit numbers is a reasonable Quarter 1 demand, and the contextual versions about counting seashells or stickers collected by friends stay short enough not to add a reading burden.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Two situations alternate, a bare list of numbers to arrange and a collection story where several friends' counts must be ordered, and the set sizes and direction are shuffled independently of each other.

competency_alignment.rationale: The later seeds tighten the gaps between the values, with sets such as 404, 406, 399, 409 turning on the final digit, which is exactly the discrimination this competency is meant to build.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Values run from the thirties up to exactly 1000 and never past it, which matches the stated ceiling and still gives a spread of magnitudes.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The ordinal language itself is handled in both surface forms, with items asking for the word describing a position and others asking for the symbol, and one item places named children in a row so a position must be located.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Positions from second through twentieth are sampled, in word form and symbol form, and in both directions: naming the ordinal for a given number and identifying which position follows another.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Single-step ordinal recognition with no arithmetic beyond adding one to a position suits the first quarter of Grade 2, and the row of six named children is short enough to hold in mind.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Most items name a position in the abstract; only the row-of-children item and the arrival-order item attach an ordinal to actual objects or people, which is what describing the position of objects calls for.

competency_alignment.rationale: The comparison item asking who arrived earlier offers 16th, 7th and 8th as alternatives when the stem mentions only two places, so three of its four options are impossible and the item collapses to a coin flip that needs no ordinal reasoning.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: No position above twentieth is used anywhere in the set, and the item asking what follows 19th lands exactly on the stated ceiling rather than crossing it.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: This competency deliberately separates the place value of a digit from the value of a digit, and the generator collapses them. Three items ask what the place value of a digit is and then key a quantity: 80 for the 8 in 285, 200 for the 2 in 250, 60 for the 6 in 160. The stem asks for one thing and the key answers another, in the exact node where the distinction is being introduced.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: All three sub-cases the wording lists do get generated somewhere: naming the place a digit occupies, giving the quantity a digit stands for, and returning the digit that sits in a stated place.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Three-digit numbers with one digit probed per item, including the harder zero cases in 260 and 405, is the right level; no stem asks about more than one digit at a time.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Five of the eleven samples are true-or-false items that simply restate a candidate answer and ask for a verdict, which converts an open place-value question into a yes-or-no check and removes the need to generate the answer.

competency_alignment.rationale: Because the term used in the stem does not stay fixed to the term the key answers, a pupil working through the harder seeds cannot extract a stable rule; the progression varies which digit is probed but leaves the vocabulary unreliable.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Every number used is three digits, as the competency specifies, with none padded out to four or reduced to two.

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The counting-up model is genuinely enacted: each item starts at a two-digit number and moves forward by a one-digit amount, and the number-line items make that hop explicit by asking where the dot lands.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Hops that stay inside a ten and hops that cross one both occur in quantity, and starting points are spread from the thirties to the nineties rather than clustering at round numbers.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: A single one-digit hop from a stated two-digit start is exactly the load this competency is written for, and the stems stay to one or two short sentences.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Five presentations appear, which is good, but all three true-or-false items are keyed False. That variant therefore rewards answering False without ever counting up, which defeats the point of including it.

competency_alignment.rationale: The difficulty ramp raises the starting number while holding the hop at a single digit, which is the right axis: the challenge in counting up is where you start, not how far you go.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: One item starts at 94 and counts up 7, landing on 101. That carries the illustration out of the two-digit territory the competency frames, and on a number-line model the crossing of a hundred is a distinctly different picture from the rest of the set.
